Markets 
A month ago, sugar market analysts were questioning whether the rally that had lifted NY11 from around 
15c/lb in July to the mid-18c/lb range by the end of September had run its course. At the time, 
speculative buying, fuelled by El Niño-related concerns, appeared to be the main driver behind the move. 
Today, however, prices are approaching the 20c/lb level, prompting a different question: are we 
overlooking a fundamental factor, or is speculative activity still the primary force behind the rally? 
Indeed, speculative buying remains a major source of support for the market. As of 20 October, the net 
speculative long position had reached 223,000 lots, close to the highest level in five years, although still 
well below the all-time high of 348,000 lots recorded in October 2016. We continue to believe that specs 
are unlikely to become meaningful sellers before February, when they will face the decision of either 
rolling their positions forward or taking profits and reducing their exposure. Regardless of how funds 
ultimately manage these positions, however, several fundamental developments are beginning to emerge 
that could help explain the latest leg higher in prices.

crushing activity is likely to be significantly disrupted, potentially leaving Brazil C/S with its lowest 
monthly cane crush since the 2021/22 season, when total crop crushing reached just 523mmt. 
The impact of the recent rainfall was one of the main topics of discussion during London Sugar Week, 
leading several analysts to revise their Brazil C/S sugar production estimates to below 38 Mt. Interestingly, 
traditional variables such as cane area and agricultural yields received relatively little attention, as 
concerns over cane availability appear limited. Looking further ahead, the combination of abundant cane 
availability and sustained rainfall should provide favourable conditions for crop development during the 
first half of the 2027/28 season. The outlook for the second half will depend more heavily on summer 
rainfall, which could remain supportive under an El Niño pattern. Overall, weather permitting, Brazil C/S 
looks increasingly likely to test the limits of its crushing capacity next season. 
Before getting there, however, the market still needs to navigate disappointing Northern Hemisphere 
crops. With the exception of China and Russia, most major Northern Hemisphere producers are currently 
facing dry conditions, with India emerging as the key concern. 
Following a series of policy measures, including an 1mmt duty free import quota that ultimately allowed 
only 250 kt of sugar into the domestic market, the Indian government succeeded in stabilising prices 
during September. Nevertheless, the underlying supply-and-demand imbalance remains unresolved, as 
suggested by extension of the deadline for duty-free raw sugar imports by two months that has been 
informed by the government this week.  
The new Indian crushing season has only just begun, with progress in some states being hampered by 
farmer protests, though the early start should show higher October figures when compared to the past 
crop. As in Brazil C/S, production expectations have also been revised lower following recent field 
assessments conducted by several trade houses. Overall, India enters the season with sugar production 
expectations of around 27mmt, a level that, in our view, is likely to necessitate another import quota in 
the coming months. The timing of any additional imports will ultimately depend on early crop 
performance and the behaviour of domestic sugar prices.  
Brazil’s ethanol balance is also tightening. August and September data show hydrous ethanol consumption 
approaching 1.8 million cbm. Meanwhile, exports remained substantial in September, at around 350,000 
cbm — approximately 170,000 cbm above the previous month and 76% higher year on year. Strong 
domestic demand, combined with the crop reduction mentioned above, could drive ethanol ending stocks 
to low levels by the end of the season, providing price support for the biofuel and, indirectly, influencing 
sugar prices as sugar mix potential decreases in the following Brazil C/S crop.

3

To make matters more complicated, the recent Brazilian election resulted in Lula securing re-election 
after losing the first round. Concerns over fiscal discipline led the market to interpret the outcome 
negatively for the Brazilian economy, triggering a sharp depreciation of the BRL. This, in turn, weighed 
heavily on the sugar market, with NY11 falling by more than 100 points in a single session following the 
election result. 
A weaker BRL could become one of the main bearish risks for sugar, as it improves local currency returns 
for Brazilian producers and could increase the incentive to maximise sugar production. As a result, the 
market will be closely watching the formation of the new government, particularly the appointment of 
the new Economy Minister and the direction of fiscal policy, for clues on the outlook for the Brazilian 
economy and the BRL in 2027. 
Overall, speculators are likely to remain the main driver of the market in the near term, although 
fundamentals are also gradually shifting in a more bullish direction. Brazilian political developments, 
however, remain an important source of uncertainty and could still bring surprises. Looking into the 
medium term, Brazil’s large 2027/28 crop does not appear to be under threat at this stage. However, 
even a strong Brazilian crop may not be sufficient to fully offset the production losses the market is 
currently anticipating elsewhere in 2027. 
Fundamentals  
➢ India: Rainfall across the key cane-growing regions of central-west India has been significantly below normal, 
materially weakening the outlook for both the 2026/27 and 2027/28 sugar seasons. Cumulative rainfall in 
Maharashtra and Karnataka, which account for approximately 36% and 18% of India’s sugar production, 
respectively, is currently 30% and 34% below normal. More importantly, the rainfall shortfall has been 
particularly severe in the districts that typically drive production swings. In Maharashtra, cumulative rainfall 
has been 58% below normal in Solapur, 47% below normal in Marathwada and 55% below normal in Nagar. A 
similar pattern has emerged in Karnataka, where rainfall is 30% below normal in Bagalkot, 48% below normal 
in Bijapur, 59% below normal in Kalaburagi, 37% below normal in Bidar and 55% below normal across southern 
Karnataka. Overall, the rainfall deficit affecting the cane-growing areas of central-west India is more severe 
than that recorded during the 2015/16 season. The prolonged dryness has reduced available soil moisture and 
adversely affected cane development, agricultural yields and sugar recovery. Crushing operations have already 
started in Maharashtra, with approximately 100 mills currently operating. Initial feedback from harvested 
farms  point to lower cane yields and reduced cane availability. As a result, the 2026/27 crushing season is 
expected to be unusually short, with some mills likely to begin closing from the first week of December as local 
cane supplies are exhausted. Against estimated 2026/27 sugar production close to 27.0mmt and domestic 
consumption of 28.5mmt, India is expected to require total imports during the season. Even with imports, 
stocks at the end of September 2027 are estimated to be a relatively tight. The consequences of the rainfall 
deficit are likely to extend into the following season. The significant deterioration in soil moisture, combined 
with weaker returns and reduced cane availability for planting, is expected to lead to a substantial contraction 
in harvested area in 2027/28. Despite the increasingly constructive supply outlook, domestic sugar prices 
remained broadly stable week on week. Ex-mill prices are currently trading at approximately INR 47,000–
47,500 per metric tonne in central-west India and INR 49,000–49,500 per metric tonne in North India. The 
higher northern premium reflects regional supply conditions, while prices in central-west India have yet to

fully incorporate the potential severity of the emerging cane shortage. Overall, the rainfall deficit has shifted 
India’s sugar outlook from a weak 2026/27 crop to a potentially more structural two-season supply problem. 
Lower yields and a shortened crushing season are expected to constrain production in 2026/27, while reduced 
acreage could push output materially lower in 2027/28. If confirmed, this would transform India from a 
marginal import requirement in 2026/27 into a major buyer of Brazilian raw sugar in 2027/28, providing an 
important source of support to the global trade balance. 
 
➢ Asia: The recovery in late-September rainfall in Thailand has eased concerns over a severe El Niño impact on 
the upcoming sugarcane crop. In September, rainfall across most regions ranged from 1% to 97% above both 
2025 levels and the 10-year historical averages. The North-east was the only exception, recording a saw a 16% 
decline compared to 2025. While the improved rainfall has partially alleviated drought concerns, the main 
question remains as to whether the timing or distribution of the rainfall is sufficient and appropriate for the 
cane. Concerns over intense rainfall concentration in short periods of time may cause waterlogging, which 
would have a detrimental effect on the crop. October saw relatively dryer conditions throughout Thailand. As 
of 18th Oct, only Central rainfall saw 33% YoY higher than last year’s, with the remaining 3 regions receiving 
approximately 50% less than 2025. On a cumulative basis, total rainfall to date since January is at 1096mm, 
falling short of last year’s 1314mm.  At this point of writing, it is likely we might not see such a heavy impact 
on the crop referencing those drought years in 2015 and 2019, since current rainfall has exceeded those years. 
In other smaller Asia producing regions like the Philippines and Vietnam, production should drop by 7-10% 
compared to 2025 considering a moderate El Nino impact. In Philippines, growing reports of RSSI diseases 
have added concerns to lower cane yields and production, which may pose further downside risks to the 
current crop. 
 
➢ US: The October WASDE brought fewer changes to the US S&D than last month. The main revision was a 44k 
MTRV cut to domestic deliveries for both crops, reflecting the weak performance of deliveries so far, which 
USDA carried over into the 2026/27 projection. For the 2025/26 crop, beet sugar production was revised down 
by 34k MTRV, but the main changes came from imports: re-exports were up 54k MTRV to 362k MTRV, and 
TR2 was up 76k MTRV to 1,045k MTRV, with TR2 expected to keep being revised up in the coming reports. For 
the 2026/27 crop, besides the lower deliveries, beet production was cut by another 24k MTRV. All in all, the 
2026/27 Stock To Use (STU) now at 14.9%, above the 13.5% target set under the Suspension Agreement, which 
represents a surplus of around 160k MTRV. There are no updates yet on the impact of the mealybug on Florida 
cane fields, but with the harvest just getting started, we should start to hear more soon. 
 
➢ Mexico:  Conadesuca first crop projection for the crop 26/27 shows sugar output at 5.3mmt, basically the 
same value of the previous season. Cane area is expected at 782k ha with agricultural yields pegged at 
62.3ton/ha, resulting in a cane crush of 48.7mmt. USDA view for the new crop is higher with a sugar output 
projected at 5.4mmt. 
 
➢ Centrals: The region is still in its intercrop period, with the 2026/27 crop expected to start over the next few 
weeks. Weather conditions remain concerning across the region which should results in 10% drop YoY in the 
sugar output, with individual countries ranging from 5% to 20% reductions YoY. There are still signs that 
production could deteriorate further, so additional cuts can't be ruled out. 
 
➢ EU/UK: The dry weather has run on into the campaign, and the first lifting results have confirmed the cuts 
producers made to their estimates in September. September rainfall finished well below the five-year norm 
across the western beet belt, with France receiving 21mm against the historical average of 73mm, Belgium 
30mm against 78mm, Germany 30mm against 89mm and the UK 25mm against 80mm, while the Netherlands 
received 70mm against 76mm. From 3 to 21 October France received 31mm against a norm of 41mm, Belgium 
29mm against 42mm, Germany 31mm against 33mm, the UK 38mm against 53mm and Poland 11mm against 
27mm. The French ministry of agriculture on 13 October lowered its 2026 beet forecast to 25.3mmt from

25.4mmt, 30% lower on the year and the lowest since its records began in 1980. The CGB on 17 September 
put the area that will not be harvested at 20,000ha, up from 3,000ha a week earlier, with Île-de-France, 
Champagne, the Yonne, the Aube, Centre-Val de Loire, Alsace, the Oise and the Eure the worst affected, and 
some producers expect yields 25% lower than last year. In Germany, WVZ on 6 October lowered its 2026/27 
sugar estimate to 3.33mmt from 3.386mmt in September, 25% lower on the year, on 299,970ha against 
348,678ha, a beet yield of 71.2mt/ha against 82.1mt/ha and a sugar yield of 11.1mt/ha against 12.7mt/ha, 
with sugar content unchanged at 17.6%. Rhineland-Palatinate reports a beet yield of 41mt/ha and a sugar 
yield of 7.5mt/ha so far, its weakest since 1991. In Poland,  producers had lifted 20,000ha by mid-October with 
beet yields below last year but above the long-term average and sugar content at 16%. KGS has withdrawn its 
plan to cut 2027 contract area by 10% but kept its beet offer at EUR 26/mt, which the growers’ association 
KZPBC says is below cost, with talks resuming in November. Netherlands producers reported 15.8% sugar 
content in the first three weeks of the Dutch campaign and has extended processing by about a week with no 
change to expected output. In the UK, producers began slicing at Wissington on 29 September and at Bury St 
Edmunds and Newark on 6 October, with Cantley to start its final campaign on 10 November; yields are 
variable after the drought and sugar content is running above expectations, and British Sugar and NFU Sugar 
settled the 2027/28 contract on 5 October at GBP 28.50/mt fixed for up to half of contract tonnage, (against 
GBP 30/mt this year), or a GBP 25.50/mt base plus a market-linked bonus. 
 
➢ East Europe: Russia’s campaign is running at a strong pace, the season’s output forecasts have moved up 
rather than down, and the smaller EAEU markets are tightening import controls to protect their own 
producers. The Eurasian Sugar Association put Russian sugar output at 2.43mmt as of 13 October. Krasnodar 
factories turned out 413kmt in the first eight months of the year, 20% more than in the same period of 2025, 
according to the regional agriculture ministry. Sugar.ru now sees 2026/27 Russian output at 6.9mmt once the 
syrup and molasses runs are counted, well above the Bank of Russia’s 6.3mmt, which rests on yield gains 
making good the smaller area. Sugar.ru also reported that a number of plants are not slicing at full rate, with 
molasses hard to place and tanks full. Russian retail sugar averaged RUB 85/kg (USD 1.01/kg) in September, 
16% above a year earlier. Kyrgyzstan’s agriculture ministry said on 14 October that a six-month halt to sugar 
imports would take effect within a fortnight; Sugar.ru estimated that 20kmt had already arrived from Russia 
by mid-October. Belarus has produced 280kmt so far this campaign and Belgospischeprom expects to finish 
above 700kmt. 
Focus – Brazil C/S  
According to MAPA figures, by the end of September, CS mills had crushed 482mmt of cane, 1.6% behind last year. 
Sugar output was 28.9mmt, down 13.6% YoY, with a sugar mix of 47.0% against 52.3% LY. Total ethanol production, 
from both cane and corn, was 7% higher. The cane availability is not what will define the rest of the season. Agricultural 
yields have been good and there is plenty of cane left in the fields. The final number depends on how many days the 
rains will allows mills to keep crushing. 
Weather has been the main driver since September. Centre South has lost about 6 crushing days due to rains in 
September (vs 2.4 days average) while crush was down 20% YoY as a result (MAPA). The worst-hit states were MS (10 
days lost vs 3.5 normally, crush down 30%), PR (9.5 days vs 4, crush down 50%), and SP (6 days vs 2.4, crush down 
23%, or 11mmt). October has been just as wet, with almost 12 days lost (vs. historical average with 5). This is the 
regional pattern a strong El Niño tends to bring, with wetter conditions in the south and southeast, and the current 
event is forecast to be among the strongest on record.

November is still expected to be wetter than normal, with forecasts pointing to around 10 days lost to rain up to Nov 
25th (vs. about 7 historically). With so much cane still in the fields, mills should keep running at full capacity finishing 
their crop later than usual, with several mills harvesting until close to Christmas. On that basis, the CS could crush 
about 150mmt from October until the end of March, weather permitting, which brings the season near the 630mmt 
forecasted. That would be the second-largest crush after September in the past decade, what makes it quite 
challenging but achievable. As cane is not the constraint, the risks run both ways. A drier-than-normal end to the 
season would push the crush above 630mmt, while each additional day lost to rain would costs more crush. Any cane 
left in the field will carry over into 2027/28 and support the start of next season. Late-season rain would also dilute 
ATR, which is already suffering great losses this season. After a more ethanol-oriented start of the season, the current 
price parities between sugar and ethanol leaves no doubt and the producer is focusing on sugar production at a great 
extent, although the rains also have a negative influence on this point. In any case, CS should still see sugar output 
close to 37mmt.
